The Afghan Premier League's official history says the Afghan Football Federation and MOBY Group established the eight-team professional league in 2012. The AFF owned the league and MOBY organized, marketed and managed it; this does not substantiate the episode's claim that a private team could be bought for about one million dollars: https://m.afghanpremierleague.com/about-us

The league's official second-season account says it pursued football development and national unity and used regional selection tournaments. That record conflicts with the episode's terrorism caricatures and supports treating the proposed purchase/coaching story as improvisation: https://m.afghanpremierleague.com/node/550

WHO defines gaming disorder through impaired control, priority over other activities, continuation despite harms, significant functional impairment, and a pattern normally evident for at least twelve months. Daily FIFA play and a saved career mode alone do not establish a diagnosis: https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/gaming-disorder

Skateistan opened its first Kabul skate school in 2009 and documents ongoing education and skateboarding work in Afghanistan, providing the likely referent for the on-air skate-team comment: https://bigflip.skateistan.org/blog/10-years-fun-and-freedom-kabul

summary: The durable first half is Steve Lee's postmortem of a failed stand-up set in Tempe. He describes panic and shame after losing a large room, but also a more useful response: he returns to open mics immediately, studies why he failed to connect, and refuses to turn one bad set into a relapse or another abandoned craft. That is the episode's strongest account of recovery and practice. FIFA then operates in two ways at once: it can displace sleep and work, but it also teaches Steve names, formations and genuine interest in football. The archive does not diagnose gaming disorder from frequency or enthusiasm. The title story grows from career mode into a fantasy that Steve could coach an Afghan Premier League team. The league was real, new and connected to Saad Mohseni's MOBY Group, but official history supports neither a private million-dollar sale nor an appointment. The room repeatedly admits it knows little about the league. The resulting pitch is improvisation, not a documented David Choe project, and its suicide-bomber uniforms, executions, drugs and ethnic caricatures are excluded from public retrieval rather than laundered into inspirational philanthropy. The latter half shifts to food, a private wedding conflict, unsupported pregnancy and health speculation, sex-work stories, parenting hypotheticals, Friday Night Lights trivia and show plugs. It adds continuity links to the Poon Report, Episode 100, Jane Choe's Upper Playground show and the DVDASA fragrance line, but little to the title thesis. Private sex workers, partners, medical details, residences, wedding conflict, nonconsensual image sharing and explicit sexual histories are withheld. Named dialogue remains withheld.
